A Potential Probiotic Candidate Heyndrickxia ginsengihumi W1 is Associated with Increased Intestinal Stem Cell-Mediated Proliferation and Altered Barrier-Related Parameters: Potential Involvement of the Wnt/β-Catenin Pathway
abstract: Probiotic properties of the rumen-derived strain Heyndrickxia ginsengihumi W1 were evaluated by whole-genome analysis, in vitro assays, and a short-term mouse model. Genome analysis preliminarily indicated no acquired antimicrobial resistance genes or virulence factors. In mice, W1 administration showed no obvious adverse effects under the present short-term experimental conditions, and was associated with Lactobacillus enrichment and elevated lactate in the jejunum. W1 administration was also associated with changes in selected jejunal barrier-related parameters and with increased intestinal stem cell (ISC)-mediated epithelial proliferation, potentially through the Wnt/β-catenin pathway. Jejunal lactate correlated positively with crypt depth, PCNA, ISC markers, and Wnt/β-catenin components. In vitro, purified lactate and W1 cell-free supernatant, but not heat-killed W1, promoted sheep intestinal epithelial cell proliferation, and lactate upregulated Axin2, Ctnnb1, and PCNA, but this lactate-Wnt/β-catenin mechanism remains a hypothesis requiring further validation. These results indicate that W1 may be a promising rumen-derived probiotic candidate.

title: Isolation, characterization, and ecotoxicological testing of aquaculture-native bacterial antagonists against the fish pathogen Flavobacterium psychrophilum
abstract: Intensive aquaculture is experiencing bottlenecks due to diseases caused by bacterial pathogens, such as, the agent of Bacterial Cold-Water Disease and Rainbow Trout Fry Syndrome in salmonids. With rising antimicrobial resistance and limited vaccine efficacy, biocontrol alternatives are needed. Here, we developed an integrated screening pipeline to isolate native bacterial antagonists offrom a rainbow trout recirculating aquaculture system. Combining an agar-based inhibition assay,antimicrobial resistance, and virulence screening, and ecotoxicity evaluation towardand, we identified three-antagonizing strains with favorable preliminary safety profiles:BG17,IW15, andsp. CB21. Cell-free supernatants of these isolates suppressedgrowth, with concentration-dependent effects for CB21 and IW15, and across the tested supernatant dilution range for BG17. Growth of antagonists in 50 μM and 200 μM FeClreduced pathogen inhibition by BG17 across all supernatant concentrations. Its iron-free supernatant absorbed near 405 nm and fluoresced at 440-445 nm, while direct FeCladdition shifted both signals, and growth of the antagonist in extra iron reduced them. Together with an NRPS cluster of low similarity to a characterized pyoverdine biosynthetic gene cluster (BGC) and a positive CAS assay, these findings are consistent with an iron-responsive fluorescent chelator in BG17. The effect of iron on the inhibition caused by IW15 supernatant differed depending on the iron concentration tested, suggesting a more complex iron-responsive phenotype rather than a simple concentration-dependent effect. Inhibition by CB21 supernatant was not significantly affected by iron under the tested conditions, and its genome did not encode a dedicated siderophore BGC. These aquaculture-native isolates inhibitthrough apparently distinct mechanisms and warrant further evaluation as biocontrol candidates.IMPORTANCEWorldwide production of intensively farmed salmonids in aquaculture represents a valuable source of high-quality protein but is challenged by significant losses caused by bacterial pathogens, such as. On a global scale, outbreaks are treated with antibiotics, leading to the development of antimicrobial resistance, while farm effluents can spread resistant bacteria into surrounding freshwater ecosystems, even reaching human pathogens with clinical relevance. Safer biocontrol alternatives are necessary, and probiotics have gained interest as a promising option. Here, we describe three native bacterial strains from a rainbow trout farming environment that through apparently distinct mechanisms inhibit the testedstrain. The strains were selected via combined genomic safety and ecotoxicity screening on non-target eukaryotic organisms. By integrating functional, genomic safety, and environmental criteria early in thescreening process, this study advances a One Health approach to develop sustainable disease management alternatives for aquaculture.

title: Detection of single nucleotide polymorphism-based macrolide resistance via multiplex mediator displacement loop-mediated isothermal amplification in Treponema pallidum
abstract: Single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) can drive antimicrobial resistance (AMR). Genotypic detection offers a rapid alternative to phenotypic testing, particularly for(), but remains challenging in resource-limited or field settings. Isothermal methods, such as loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP), are increasingly being used in molecular diagnostics. Given the cost advantages of LAMP over PCR, extending this approach to technically challenging applications such as SNP detection is highly relevant. Although conventional LAMP lacks intrinsic single-base discrimination, several strategies have been developed to enable point mutation detection. We present a multiplex mediator displacement (MD) LAMP assay with internal control (IC) to differentiate two neighboring SNPs associated with macrolide resistance (MR) from wild-type 23S rRNA sequence in. We further introduce a novel fluorogenic universal reporter with approximately 459 nm blue emission spectrum. The assay achieved limits of detection of 944, 57, and 43 copies per reaction for A2058G, A2059G, and wild-type, respectively. High specificity for A2058G was obtained by incorporating an additional mismatch in loop primer design. No cross-reactivity was observed against 15 non-target pathogens. Assessment with 43 genomic syphilis DNA samples from human skin ulcers confirmed analytical performance and applicability of developed assay and resulted in moderate-to-high concordance between PCR and LAMP (Cohen's kappa coefficient= 0.65). These demonstrate that TPMR MD LAMP is a rapid, sensitive, and specific approach for multiplex genotypic AMR detection.

title: Characterization of potential probiotic Lactobacillus spp. isolated from commercially reared pigs
abstract: Probiotic bacteria and their products have shown significant promise as alternatives to traditional antimicrobials in the pig husbandry due to their antimicrobial activity. This study describes the comprehensive characterization of potential probiotic isolates sourced from the feces of commercial pig herds. Using high-throughput screening methodologies, sequential tests were performed, and isolates were discarded following any failure to meet a test acceptance criterion, allowing the initial 81 isolates collected to be reduced to 18 probiotic candidates in five screening steps. Whole-genome sequencing of 20 isolates revealed only 6 harbored previously reported antibiotic resistance genes and provided detailed taxonomic information. However,susceptibility testing highlighted much higher levels of antibiotic resistance, with only two isolates showing noresistance, one isolate with resistance to chloramphenicol only, and all other isolates tested (= 26) having resistance to two or more antibiotics. Moreover,inhibition assays demonstrated that supernatants from 11 isolates significantly (≤ 0.05) decreased growth ofNCTC 13441 and ATCC 25922,Typhimurium NCTC 12023, andTyphimurium SL1344, with much of the activity lost after pH adjustment. Attachment ofandTyphimurium to intestinal cells was also significantly reduced (≤ 0.05) following preincubation with probiotic isolate P-001-01. In conclusion, pig-derived lactic acid-producing bacteria are promising candidates for probiotic use. However, carefulscreening of antibiotic susceptibility is required as high levels of antibiotic resistance may be present without corresponding known antibiotic resistance gene presence.IMPORTANCENew, non-antibiotic options are needed to limit post-weaning diarrhea and weight loss in commercial pig herds. Probiotic supplements have shown promise in achieving this, but a greater number of candidate probiotic strains are required, and their isolation and characterization can be a costly and lengthy process. Here, we describe a rapid, high-throughput, and cost-effective workflow for the isolation and characterization of probiotic species obtained from existing healthy pig herds. Using this workflow, we isolated and characterized a large number of lactic acid-producing bacterial isolates. Many of the isolates we obtained had high phenotypic levels of antimicrobial resistance although, for many of the isolates, there was a poor correlation between phenotypic and genotypic resistance. The results presented here highlight that while many lactic acid bacteria isolates are present within the feces of pigs from commercial herds, very few of the isolates meet the stringent guidelines required for commercial probiotic isolates.

title: Serum procalcitonin in the assessment of febrile neutropenia in hematological patients
abstract: This review focuses on recent literature of the use of procalcitonin (PCT) to assess infection severity and prognosis in hematological patients with chemotherapy-induced febrile neutropenia (FN). A substantial proportion of patients with hematological malignancies receive intensive chemotherapy, which often leads to neutropenia, associated with infectious complications, and prolonged use of antibiotics. Antimicrobial resistance is a growing problem with far-reaching consequences, and hematological patients undergoing chemotherapy are at a particularly high risk. Observational studies indicate that PCT concentration 0.1-0.5 μg/L suggests localized infection; systemic infection is unlikely when PCT <0.1 μg/L, and likely when PCT ≥2 μg/L. In sepsis studies utilizing PCT-guided therapy, the threshold values used at the initiation of treatment range from 0.10 to 0.5 μg/L. The commonly used criteria for discontinuation include 50 % reduction from the previous value, 65 % decrease within three days, or ≥80-90 % decrease from the peak value. Of note, these cut-offs are based on early clinical studies and do not consider variable analysis methods available. When these thresholds are applied to sepsis patients, the duration of treatment is typically reduced by approximately two days. Some studies have reported reduction in antibiotic-related adverse effects and antimicrobial resistance, and even a decrease in mortality. Further experience and data are needed regarding PCT-guided management in hematological patients with chemotherapy-induced FN. Findings of observational studies largely support the utility of PCT measurements in chemotherapy-induced FN, but there is a paucity of interventional studies evaluating the use of PCT algorithms in FN patients and the results are inconsistent.

title: CRISPR/Cas-Mediated Genome Editing in Azotobacter vinelandii and Stutzerimonas stutzeri
abstract: The Gammaproteobacteria Azotobacter vinelandii and Stutzerimonas stutzeri are widely used model organisms for studying biological nitrogen metabolism. In the context of climate change and environmental pollution, they show promise as biofertilizers and in reducing soil nitrification. However, current genomic manipulation methods predominantly rely on the introduction of antibiotic resistance, which might lead to the emergence of multidrug-resistant strains. Here, we report the development of versatile, single-plasmid CRISPR systems for markerless genome editing in A. vinelandii and S. stutzeri. We demonstrate that CRISPR/Cas9 and CRISPR/Cas12a systems efficiently mediate genomic deletions, insertions, and substitutions, with the choice of system dictated by the targeted PAM sequence. We show that, in A. vinelandii, the use of separate linear repair templates instead of plasmid-borne repair templates significantly reduces undesired plasmid incorporation resulting from single-crossover events. Following this approach, a strain of A. vinelandii expressing fluorescent rsLOV2-tagged nitrogenase was constructed and characterized. This construct enabled the spatiotemporal localization of nitrogenase in live cells, demonstrating the rapid expression and cellular distribution of nitrogenase as cells transition into diazotrophy. The genome editing platform described in this study accelerates the comprehensive engineering of A. vinelandii for biotechnological applications, while also advancing our understanding of nitrogenase systems.

title: Bacterial etiology and antimicrobial resistance patterns of urinary tract infections in Beni Mellal, Morocco
abstract: The emergence of multidrug-resistant pathogens responsible for both nosocomial and community-acquired urinary tract infections (UTIs) has critically compromised empirical therapeutic pathways for clinicians. This study aimed to evaluate the epidemiology and antimicrobial resistance patterns of uropathogens causing UTIs in both outpatients and hospitalized patients, encompassing children, adults, and older adults, referred to the Regional Hospital Center (RHC) of Beni Mellal, Morocco, between January and December 2018. A total of 800 cytobacteriological examinations of urine (ECBU) were analyzed, and the isolated uropathogens were evaluated for their susceptibility to various antimicrobial agents. A total of 116 (14.5%) UTI/ECBU samples were positive, with a higher frequency observed in females (60.4%). UTIs were more frequent in outpatients (66.4%) than in hospitalized patients (33.6%). The highest frequencies were noted among females and older adults, followed by adults and children. Among the identified uropathogens, Enterobacteriaceae accounted for 97.7% of the isolates. Similar frequencies of Escherichia coli (E. coli) were observed between outpatients (75.3%) and hospitalized patients (71.8%), whereas Klebsiella pneumoniae (K. pneumoniae) showed a higher frequency in hospitalized individuals (25.6%). Additionally, Proteus mirabilis, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Staphylococcus aureus were isolated from UTI patients, albeit in lower frequencies. Escherichia coli isolates displayed high phenotypic susceptibility to mecillinam (MEC), piperacillin/tazobactam (TZP), cefoxitin (FOX), and trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole (SXT), while Klebsiella pneumoniae isolates were highly susceptible to TZP, cefotaxime (CTX), FOX, MEC, ciprofloxacin (CIP), and SXT. Conversely, E. coli isolates exhibited phenotypic resistance to ticarcillin (TIC), amoxicillin (AMX), cefotaxime (CTX), nalidixic acid (NA), amoxicillin/clavulanic acid (AMC), and ciprofloxacin (CIP), whereas K. pneumoniae isolates were resistant to AMX, TIC, AMC, and NA. In this study UTIs remain a primary driver of bacterial infections within the Beni Mellal-Khenifra region. While, Escherichia coli was the predominant pathogen across both outpatients and hospitalized patients, Klebsiella pneumoniae showed a distinctively higher prevalence in hospital settings. Escherichia coli isolat​es displayed high phenotypic susceptibility to mecillinam (MEC), piperacillin-tazobactam (TZP), cefoxitin (FOX), and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (SXT), and phenotypic resistance to ticarcillin (TIC), amoxicillin (AMX), cefotaxime (CTX), nalidixic acid (NA), amoxicillin/clavulanic acid (AMC), and ciprofloxacin (CIP), Whereas, Klebsiella pneumoniae isolates were highly susceptible to TZP, cefotaxime (CTX), FOX, MEC, ciprofloxacin (CIP), and SXT, and resistant to AMX, TIC, AMC, and NA. Other uropathogens, including Proteus mirabilis, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Staphylococcus aureus, were also identified, though at lower frequencies. These epidemiological insights provide a crucial foundation for optimizing empirical therapy, reducing regional UTI incidence, and curbing antimicrobial resistance. Ultimately, this work establishes a baseline for future regional surveillance, directly contributing to the development of Morocco's national resistance map.

title: Cis genetic variation drives gene expression changes in the E. coli and P. aeruginosa pangenomes
abstract: Bacteria use gene regulation to dynamically adapt to changes in their environment, including resistance to stress and the occupation of new niches. Gene expression is known to vary within a species pangenome, but the extent to which these changes could be explained by genetic variants in cis regulatory regions has so far been poorly investigated. Statistical genetics offers a hypothesis-free approach to this problem, as opposed to mechanistic models, which can be used only for reference isolates that are not representative of the whole species. In this study, we assembled two genomic and transcriptomic datasets for Escherichia coli (N = 117) and Pseudomonas aeruginosa (N = 413) and identified associations between genetic variants in cis regulatory regions and recorded gene expression variation. We identified at least one associated variant in up to 39% of the tested genes in both species. We partly validated the associations in-silico and in-vitro for E. coli, reinforcing the difficulty of identifying a single mechanism generating gene expression diversity. We then investigated the relevance of regulatory variants in explaining the variability in antimicrobial resistance in both species using two additional publicly available datasets, identifying a large number of these variants across antimicrobial compounds. This work, which is the first cis-eQTL study for bacterial species, confirms the role of genetic variation in often overlooked regions of bacterial genomes in influencing molecular and clinically relevant phenotypes.

title: Molecular Characteristics and Antimicrobial Resistance of Vibrio parahaemolyticus Isolated from Aquatic Products in Huzhou, China
abstract: Vibrio parahaemolyticus (V. parahaemolyticus) is a major pathogen responsible for seafood-associated gastroenteritis worldwide. In recent years, the number of infections caused by this bacterium has shown a significant increasing trend globally. In this study, antimicrobial susceptibility testing and whole-genome sequencing were performed on 150 strains of V. parahaemolyticus isolated from 1,111 aquatic product samples collected in Huzhou area in 2025. Multilocus sequence typing (MLST), resistance gene profiling, virulence gene analysis, and genetic relatedness assessment were conducted using bioinformatics approaches. A total of 23 serotypes were identified among the 150 strains, with the most common being O2:KUT (18.00%), O2:K28 (13.30%), and O1:KUT (12.67%). The 150 strains were classified into 81 sequence types (STs), showing a relatively scattered distribution. The strains exhibited varying degrees of resistance to most antibiotics, with the highest resistance rate observed against colistin (CT, 84.00%). Multidrug resistance was frequently observed among the isolates in this study. A total of 31 resistance-related genes belonging to nine classes were detected, with β-lactam resistance genes being predominant. Additionally, 192 virulence genes were identified; all isolates carried the tlh gene, but neither tdh nor trh was detected. Furthermore, all isolates carried effector proteins associated with T3SS1. Phylogenetic analysis based on core gene trees indicated that serotyping was highly correlated with the genetic background of the core genome, and the strains exhibited a multi-branch, multi-lineage co-existing structure across geographical regions and isolation sources, without forming a single predominant clonal group.Huzhou seafood V. parahaemolyticus shows high cephalosporin/multidrug resistance and genetic heterogeneity; all lacked tdh/trh but carried T3SS1, so resistance and virulence genomics should inform risk monitoring.

title: Comparative Genomics of Complete Genomes from Non-Kp1 Species within the Klebsiella pneumoniae Species Complex: A Hidden Reservoir of Carbapenem Resistance and Virulence
abstract: The Klebsiella pneumoniae species complex (KpSC) poses a global public health threat, yet genomic studies have disproportionately focused on Klebsiella pneumoniae (Kp1), leaving the clinical and epidemiological significance of non-Kp1 species less underexplored. In this study, we analyzed a selected collection of complete genomes to identify genomic determinants associated with antimicrobial resistance (AMR) and virulence across non-Kp1 Klebsiella species. We retrieved complete non-Kp1 genomes from the NCBI database and retained 340 assemblies after stringent quality assessment. Comprehensive comparative genomic analyses were performed, encompassing distribution, phylogenomics, resistome and virulome profiling, plasmid typing, pan-genome characterization, and the genetic contexts of carbapenemase genes. Analysis of the 340 high-quality assemblies identified Klebsiella variicola subsp. variicola (Kp3) as the dominant lineage (51.5%). Klebsiella quasipneumoniae subsp. quasipneumoniae (Kp2) exhibited a high carbapenemase gene carriage (44.1%). The IncF family was the most prevalent plasmid replicon type. Phylogenomics suggested a genomic overlap across ecological distribution. Pan-genome analysis identified 129 significantly enriched genes in non-Kp1, primarily enriched in inorganic ion transport, transcription, and signal transduction. Carbapenemase genetic environments closely paralleled those found in prevalent Kp1 clones: blawas located within the canonical transposonTn4401; blawas part of a highly conserved genetic array (bla-ble-trpF-dsbD-cutA-groS-groL); and blawas conserved on a disseminated IncX3-type plasmid backbone. Non-Kp1 species may serve as potential cross-sectoral dissemination for resistance and virulence determinants, harboring traits with genomic signatures parallel to Kp1 via shared mobile genetic elements. Their metabolic specialization is hypothesized to potentially facilitate environmental persistence. These findings suggest that enhanced molecular diagnostics and integrated One Health surveillance are essential to better characterize the dissemination of these species.

title: Photodynamic Therapy for Anti-infection in Diabetic Foot Ulcers: A Review of Clinical Evidence and Practical Challenges
abstract: Infected diabetic foot ulcers (DFUs) carry high infection and amputation risks, and conventional therapies are increasingly limited by antibiotic resistance and biofilms. This review evaluated the clinical efficacy and safety of antimicrobial photodynamic therapy (aPDT) as an adjunctive treatment for infected DFUs and mapped barriers to translation. We systematically searched PubMed, Embase, Scopus, and Web of Science through January 2025 for clinical studies of aPDT in infected DFUs. Seventeen eligible studies were included, comprising randomized controlled trials (RCTs), non-randomized controlled studies, case series, and case reports. Data on protocols, outcomes, and safety were extracted and synthesized narratively; risk of bias and certainty of evidence were assessed using Cochrane Risk of Bias 2.0 and the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) framework. aPDT consistently reduced microbial burden, with a dose-dependent reduction of up to -2.94 log10 colony-forming units (CFU)/mL (p < 0.001), and promoted wound closure. One controlled study reported lower amputation rates with aPDT than with control (5.6% vs. 100%; p = 0.002). Adverse events were mainly transient local pain or burning. However, evidence certainty was low to very low because of high risk of bias, heterogeneous photosensitizers/light doses/treatment schedules, small samples, and short follow-up. Key translational barriers include non-standardized protocols, wound hypoxia, exudate, limited light penetration, and weak health-economic data. Although promising, aPDT is not yet ready for routine adoption. Priority should be given to protocol harmonization, biomarker-guided patient selection, and large pragmatic trials. This review maps the evidence and proposes a tiered research roadmap.

title: Experimental and computational study of the synergistic antibacterial effect of florfenicol-loaded iron(III)/ultrashort peptide hydrogels
abstract: Vectorization of antibiotics is a promising alternative strategy to circumvent bacterial antibiotic resistance by improving the efficacy of existing antibacterial drugs. Self-assembled small peptides can form hydrogels with high biocompatibility, degradability, and ease of synthesis, making them promising local drug delivery platforms. We previously demonstrated that Fmoc-FFpY peptides (Fmoc: fluorenylmethoxycarbonyl, F: phenylalanine; pY: tyrosine phosphate) self-assemble, in the presence of Fe, into hydrogels with ferroptosis-inducing antibacterial properties. This study describes the encapsulation and release of florfenicol (an antibiotic) by Fmoc-FFpY/Fehydrogels. We experimentally demonstrate a synergistic antibacterial effect among Fmoc-FFpY, Fe, and florfenicol. In addition to experimental validation, molecular dynamics simulations confirm that florfenicol is encapsulated within hydrogel aggregates, while suggesting that it crosses the bacterial membrane, and is retained inside bacteria. Together, these results show that encapsulating florfenicol within the peptide hydrogel enhances its activity and provides a molecular explanation for the observed synergistic antibacterial effect. This approach constitutes a promising strategy to enhance antibiotic efficacy, especially against Gram-negative bacteria.

title: Creep in Minimum Inhibitory Concentration of Commonly Used Disinfectants Against Clinical and Hospital Environmental Bacterial Isolates
abstract: Indiscriminate disinfectant use in health care settings is quietly shaping a new resistance threat. Reduced susceptibility allows hospital pathogens to persist and co-select antibiotic resistance, undermining infection control. This study focuses on the emerging and often overlooked link between disinfectant tolerance and antimicrobial resistance in bacterial isolates from clinical and hospital environments. A total of 250 clinical isolates,(50),(50),(50),(50), and(50), along with 12 outbreak-associatedand 38 environmental isolates from hospital surfaces, were included. Antimicrobial susceptibility testing was performed by the modified Kirby-Bauer disk diffusion method. Minimum inhibitory and bactericidal concentrations (minimum inhibitory concentration [MIC] and minimum bactericidal concentration [MBC]) of seven commonly used disinfectants (benzalkonium chloride, sodium hypochlorite, glutaraldehyde, chlorhexidine, hydrogen peroxide, phenol, and ethyl alcohol) were determined by macrobroth dilution. Polymerase chain reaction was employed for,, Class 1 and 2 integrons, extended-spectrum beta-lactamase (ESBL) genes (,, and), and Class B and D carbapenemase genes (,,, and). Statistical analysis was done using Fisher's exact test and Mann-Whitneytest. Multidrug resistance was observed among the clinical isolates. Disinfectants showed variable efficacy, with chlorhexidine, benzalkonium chloride, and glutaraldehyde exhibiting elevated MICs among outbreak and environmental isolates. Environmental isolates were significantly associated with higher MICs for benzalkonium chloride and glutaraldehyde (< 0.0001). Class 1 integrons were notably observed in(90%) and(78%). Among the total isolates, 56% were ESBL producers, while 67% harbored multiple Class B β-lactamase genes. No association was seen between MIC values of the tested disinfectants and resistance genes.

title: Rising Prevalence, Distinct Demographics, and Preserved Antimicrobial Susceptibility of Mucoid Pseudomonas aeruginosa-A 9-Year Single-Center Retrospective Study (2017-2025)
abstract: The mucoid phenotype ofis associated with chronic respiratory infection, biofilm formation, and antimicrobial tolerance. Its epidemiological features in general hospital populations remain poorly characterized. All non-duplicateclinical isolates recovered between 2017 and 2025 at a tertiary hospital in China were analyzed retrospectively. Mucoid phenotype was determined by colony morphology. Antimicrobial susceptibility was interpreted per CLSI breakpoints. Among 6,949 isolates, 1,932 (27.8%) were mucoid. The mucoid proportion rose from 14.0% in 2017 to 35.2% in 2025 (< 0.001). Mucoid isolates showed significantly lower resistance rates than non-mucoid isolates across all 12 anti-pseudomonal agents tested (mean fold difference 4.7). Carbapenem resistance was 11.3% versus 34.7% for imipenem and 5.5% versus 30.8% for meropenem. Ceftazidime-avibactam retained activity against 99.3% of mucoid isolates. Mucoid isolates were predominantly from female patients (62.7%), outpatient settings (59.7% mucoid), and respiratory specimens (98.2%), whereas intensive care units had the lowest mucoid proportions (1.3% to 5.4%). Mucoidin the general hospital setting represents a clinically distinct entity characterized by rising prevalence, a female-predominant outpatient demographic, and preserved antimicrobial susceptibility. Recognition of the mucoid phenotype should prompt consideration of clinical context rather than automatic concern for multidrug resistance.

title: Diphtheria Outbreak in Mali in 2025: Epidemiological and Microbial Analysis
abstract: Diphtheria remains a major public health concern. Since 2023, multiple outbreaks have been reported across the World Health Organization African Region. In 2025, Mali experienced a resurgence of diphtheria amid a prolonged security crisis and armed conflict, compounded by the long-term disruptive effects of the COVID-19 pandemic on healthcare systems. This study aimed to describe suspected and laboratory-confirmed diphtheria cases during the 2025 outbreak in Mali and to analyze the antimicrobial resistance profiles of circulating Corynebacterium diphtheriae isolates. An outbreak investigation was conducted through the national surveillance data collected from January to December 2025. Suspected cases meeting the national Integrated Disease Surveillance and Response case definitions were included. Samples were requested for all suspected cases; however, due to operational constraints, only a subset of cases underwent sample collection. Successfully collected oropharyngeal or nasopharyngeal swabs underwent laboratory testing via culture and real-time PCR targeting the rpoB and tox genes. Antimicrobial susceptibility testing was performed using the Kirby-Bauer disk diffusion method and interpreted according to EUCAST 2024 guidelines. Descriptive analyses, epidemic curves, spatial mapping, and bivariate tests were used to assess epidemiological patterns and factors associated with laboratory-confirmed cases. A total of 604 suspected diphtheria cases were reported during the investigation period, and 34 deaths were recorded corresponding to a mortality rate of 5.6%. Of these, 289 (47.8%) cases underwent laboratory testing, and 58 cases (20.1%) were laboratory confirmed. Suspected cases were reported in 36 districts across nine regions, while confirmed cases were reported across 16 districts in six regions, showing significant geographic variation. Overall, 43.3% (n = 125) of cases occurred among children aged 6-12 years. Region (p = 0.0023) and district of residence (p = 0.00003) were significantly associated with confirmed cases using chi-square tests. All toxigenic C. diphtheriae isolates were susceptible to erythromycin and clindamycin but resistant to penicillin, amoxicillin, and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, with high resistance to ciprofloxacin and tetracycline. The 2025 diphtheria outbreak in Mali highlights persistent vulnerability likely driven by subnational immunity gaps, population mobility, and emerging antimicrobial resistance. Strengthening vaccination strategies, including booster doses, expanding laboratory confirmation, and updating treatment guidelines in line with resistance patterns are critical to controlling ongoing transmission and preventing future outbreaks.

title: Challenges and opportunities in antimicrobial R&D
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance is accelerating, while the discovery and development of new drugs, particularly those with novel mechanisms of action, have failed to keep pace. This widening gap reflects two major challenges: insufficient resources for antibiotic discovery and clinical development, and a lack of scientific innovation. With pharmaceutical companies largely abandoning antibiotic R&D, academic groups, small biotech companies, and not-for-profits are stepping in, harnessing advances in genomics, synthetic biology, and AI to drive discovery. Coupled with growing international investment and initiatives to address funding gaps, these efforts offer renewed hope for overcoming the antimicrobial resistance crisis.

title: Extracellular Polymeric Substances Govern Horizontal Gene Transfer of Antibiotic Resistance Genes: Mechanisms, Pathway Specificity, and Research Gaps
abstract: The dissemination of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) in environmental systems is recognized as being shaped by local matrix conditions, yet the pathway-specific role of extracellular polymeric substances (EPS), the dominant matrix of biofilms, sludge flocs, and granules, remains poorly resolved. In this Review, we develop a mechanism- and pathway-resolved perspective for evaluating how EPS govern horizontal gene transfer (HGT) of ARGs. Current evidence indicates that conjugation is the most directly supported pathway, with EPS facilitating or restricting transfer through effects on donor-recipient contact, matrix organization, and transfer-related physiology. For transformation, EPS-associated extracellular ARGs constitute reservoirs, but EPS-DNA binding can both preserve genetic material and limit its immediate bioavailability. By contrast, EPS involvement in phage-mediated transduction and vesicle-mediated transfer remains mechanistically plausible but insufficiently validated. We identify five interconnected mechanisms: physical retention and spatial organization, DNA adsorption and bioavailability, regulation of intercellular contact, modulation of cell physiology and transfer competence, and community-scale mobilome coupling. By clarifying evidence boundaries across pathways, this Review moves EPS-HGT research from correlation-based interpretation toward mechanism-informed assessment of ARG mobility. We conclude by outlining research needs, including standardized EPS definition and extraction, component-resolved characterization, pathway-resolved causal assays, and validation in realistic environmental aggregates.

title: Genomic analysis of Klebsiella pneumoniae bloodstream isolates reveals rare hypervirulence, no convergence with antimicrobial resistance, and a bla(SHV) promoter variant associated with elevated cefiderocol MICs at a German university hospital
abstract: Hypervirulent(hvKp) and the convergence of hypervirulence with antimicrobial resistance have raised concern worldwide, but contemporary, prospective data from Central Europe remain limited. We characterizedbloodstream isolates from a German university hospital, focusing on hypervirulence and antimicrobial resistance. Bloodstream isolates were collected at University Medical Center of Schleswig-Holstein, Lübeck, Germany, between May and December 2023. In total, 74were genotyped using whole-genome sequencing. Genomic virulence and resistance determinants were characterized with Kleborate and Russo criterion. A core-genome phylogeny was reconstructed. Hypervirulence was assessed genotypically and phenotypically using string test,growth kinetics, and thekilling assay. Findings were compared against 5,514 publicly available bloodstream-derived genomes. Genomically predicted hvKp were rare (2/74 by Kleborate; 1/74 by Russo) and belonged to the classical high-risk clones ST23 and ST380, neither of which carried acquired resistance genes. Eleven isolates were resistant to third-generation cephalosporins (nine, two), and two were carbapenem-resistant through. Three isolates carried a C-112Apromoter mutation associated with elevated cefiderocol MICs (0.5-4 mg/L). Neither growth kinetics norkilling distinguished the two hypervirulent isolates from non-hypervirulent. In the public data set, the overall hvKp prevalence was low, with no significant increase between 2012 and 2025. In this cohort, hypervirulentwas rare and showed no convergence with acquired resistance. These findings suggest that convergent MDR-hvKp lineages remain uncommon and support the continued use of genomic surveillance to detect their possible future emergence. Hypervirulent(hvKp) has emerged as a major public health concern because it causes more invasive and often more severe infections than classical, and its convergence with antimicrobial resistance could further limit treatment options. However, prospective data on the prevalence of hvKp specifically from bloodstream infections remain scarce, particularly in Europe. By combining genomic analysis of a prospective bloodstream-infection cohort with more than 5,500 publicly available genomes, we show that hypervirulent strains remain uncommon and that convergence with acquired antimicrobial resistance is still rare in this setting. These findings provide an important baseline for ongoing genomic surveillance of hvKp. In addition, the same surveillance approach also flagged a previously reportedpromoter variant associated with elevated cefiderocol MICs, indicating a potential emerging mechanism that warrants further investigation as cefiderocol use becomes more widespread.

title: Genomic profiling of Salmonella enterica subsp. enterica serovar Gallinarum strains isolated from ISA brown chickens (Gallus gallus domesticus) in Bangladesh
abstract: Non-typhoidal Salmonella serotypes cause most bird salmonellosis. We isolated and sequenced sixsubsp. enterica serovar Gallinarum strains from ISA Brown chickens. The genome size was ~4.7-4.9 Mb with ~52% GC content. Core virulence architecture essential for causing fowl typhoid, along with multidrug efflux pump-dependent antibiotic resistance, was detected.

title: Ecological Resilience and Microbial Dysbiosis in the Oral Microbiome: A Systems-Level Conceptual Framework
abstract: The human oral microbiome is a highly organised, dynamic microbial ecosystem that contributes to oral homeostasis through complex interactions among microorganisms, the host immune system and the local environment. Growing evidence indicates that oral diseases are associated with ecological disruption rather than the proliferation of individual pathogens alone. Environmental perturbations, including dietary changes, poor oral hygiene, smoking, antimicrobial exposure, ageing, salivary dysfunction and systemic disorders, can alter microbial community structure, functional activity and host responses, promoting dysbiosis. Established concepts, including the ecological plaque hypothesis, keystone pathogen hypothesis and polymicrobial synergy and dysbiosis model, explain complementary aspects of oral disease development. However, an integrated framework linking cumulative environmental stress, microbial interaction networks, ecological resilience, functional changes and host-microbiome feedback remains underdeveloped. This critical narrative review synthesises evidence from microbial ecology, multi-omics, systems biology, network analysis, antimicrobial resistance and oral-systemic interactions to propose the ecological collapse model (ECM) as a hypothesis-generating conceptual framework. The ECM proposes that oral dysbiosis may develop through interacting processes of functional adaptation, ecological destabilisation and persistent community disruption. The review also examines the oral microbiome as a reservoir of antimicrobial resistance determinants and discusses potential ecological interventions, including host-response modulation, precision antimicrobials and microbiome-directed therapies. These approaches may complement established oral healthcare but require further evaluation of their efficacy, safety and durability. The ECM provides a testable framework for investigating relationships among environmental perturbation, microbial function, ecological resilience and persistent dysbiosis. Longitudinal, experimental and translational studies are needed to determine whether its proposed indicators can predict disease progression or guide microbiome-informed interventions.

title: Long-term Changes in Pediatric Non-typhoidal Salmonella Epidemiology and Antimicrobial Resistance in Taiwan
abstract: Non-typhoidal Salmonella (NTS) remains a major cause of pediatric bacterial gastroenteritis. We investigated long-term changes in serogroup distribution and antimicrobial resistance (AMR) among pediatric NTS isolates in Taiwan. This retrospective surveillance study included children (<18 years) with culture-confirmed NTS gastroenteritis. Historical serogroup data were collected at Kaohsiung Veterans General Hospital during 1996-2002 and 2009-2015, and AMR patterns were compared with a contemporary cohort from Fu Jen Catholic University Hospital during 2024-2025. Susceptibility testing used disk diffusion for historical isolates and automated broth microdilution for contemporary isolates, with interpretation according to applicable Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute standards. Serogroup B declined from 72.3% (225/311) in 1996-2002 to 46.2% (399/864) in 2009-2015, whereas serogroup D increased from 8.4% (26/311) to 32.5% (281/864). Ampicillin resistance was 60.5% and 42.6% in the historical cohorts; among 4 contemporary isolates tested, 2 were resistant (50.0%, 2/4). Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole resistance decreased from 46.1% to 16.7% and then rose to 57.1% in the contemporary cohort. Resistance to ciprofloxacin and third-generation cephalosporins was detected in 28.6% and 14.3% of contemporary isolates, respectively; all 7 contemporary isolates were susceptible to cefepime, cefoperazone-sulbactam, imipenem and ertapenem. Pediatric NTS epidemiology in Taiwan changed substantially over 2 historical surveillance periods. Resistance to ciprofloxacin and third-generation cephalosporins was detected in the small contemporary comparison cohort, supporting continued culture-based surveillance, susceptibility-guided treatment, and antimicrobial stewardship.
